subtype: Approach: sleeping properly the night before and light revision [Thinking]
passage: I'm Yogesh, and the maths exam was on Monday morning. My friend Mohit said he would stay up till midnight, and for a moment I thought I should too. Then I remembered the last late night, when my eyes stung and my mind went blank on the first question. Sleepy me will not remember anything, I thought. So at eight I read only my summary sheet, the short points I had written. Papa put down his newspaper. "Bed already, my boy?" "I'll trust what I know," I said. By half past nine, I was asleep.

qa.q: What time did Yogesh go to sleep?
qa.a: He was asleep by half past nine.

qa.q: What was Yogesh feeling as he chose to read only the summary sheet and go to bed?
qa.a: He felt confident and calm about trusting what he had learned. He remembered how bad a late night felt and did not want to repeat it.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Yogesh use if he still felt worried, and why?
qa.a: He could write down the three things he is least sure about and glance at them once. Then his worry has a small place to go and he can still sleep.

qa.q: How does Mohit's plan look next to Yogesh's?
qa.a: Mohit's plan to stay up till midnight might feel like working harder, but he could be drowsy on the first question, as Yogesh remembered feeling after a late night.

grounding: A boy decides staying up late would only make him drowsy in the exam, so he revises summary points early, sleeps by half past nine and trusts what he learned.

subtype: Approach: breaking division into smaller steps [Thinking]
passage: Fifteen minutes before the school bus, Dolma stared at the long division on Thomas Sir's worksheet. The numbers looked like knotted wool. Then she noticed something. Every sum was made of the same four jobs: divide, multiply, subtract, then bring the next digit down. It is really four small jobs, she thought. She covered the page with her hand and practised only the dividing on five sums. Then only the multiplying. Then the subtracting. At last she put them together on one sum. The bus honked outside. The answer was right, and she ran out with her bag.

qa.q: How many minutes did Dolma have before the school bus?
qa.a: She had fifteen minutes before the school bus.

qa.q: What was Dolma feeling when the numbers looked like knotted wool?
qa.a: She felt confused and a bit stressed with the bus coming. Then noticing the four jobs made her calmer.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Dolma use if the four jobs still feel hard, and why?
qa.a: She could ask a family member or Thomas Sir to show one step slowly. Seeing it done once can make her practice easier.

qa.q: How might Thomas Sir see Dolma's way of learning long division?
qa.a: Thomas Sir would probably be pleased to see a student break a hard sum into parts and practise each one. It shows the student is thinking about how to learn.

grounding: A girl finds long division confusing, sees it is four small steps, and practises each alone before joining them, even with little time.

subtype: Approach: using an everyday example to understand fractions [Thinking]
passage: Note from the tutor, Saturday. Sumit stared at three-fourths in his book and said, "It's just two numbers stuck together." His mother came out of the kitchen with a roti, cut it into four equal parts, and put three on his plate. Sumit looked at his plate, and then at the single piece left on the tray. "So the top number is how many I have," he said slowly. "And the bottom is how many parts it was cut into." He drew four boxes in his notebook and shaded three. I said nothing. He explained it to me twice. Chaitanya, tutor

qa.q: How many parts of the roti did Sumit's mother put on his plate?
qa.a: She cut it into four equal parts and put three on his plate.

qa.q: What was Sumit feeling before his mother brought the roti, and what changed?
qa.a: He was puzzled and cut off from the idea, since three-fourths seemed like two numbers stuck together. After he saw the food, he became interested and eager to explain.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Sumit use to understand other fractions, and why?
qa.a: He could fold a paper into equal parts and shade some. Seeing the parts in something he can hold makes the number less abstract.

qa.q: How might Sumit's mother see what happened at the table?
qa.a: She may feel glad that a small thing from the kitchen made her son understand. She did not explain the number, only cut the roti.

grounding: A boy cannot follow three-fourths until a roti is cut into four parts and he is given three, so real food gives the number a meaning.

subtype: Approach: memorising the rule without understanding it [Pitfall]
passage: Dear diary, I'm Diya, and today was strange. Ma'am taught us how to divide fractions: "flip and multiply." Easy! I did all twelve sums in the book and got every one right. I don't know why you flip. But it works, so who cares? Then she wrote a word problem on the board. A ribbon three-quarters of a metre long is cut into pieces one-eighth of a metre each. How many pieces? I stared. No sum, only a story. Which one do I flip? I guessed and I was wrong. Ma'am said, "Think about what the question means." I don't know what it means. Tomorrow I'll ask her.

qa.q: How many sums did Diya do in the book?
qa.a: Diya did twelve sums, and got every one right.

qa.q: What was Diya feeling when the word problem appeared on the board?
qa.a: Diya felt lost and worried. The familiar rule did not help when the question came as a story.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Diya use to understand dividing fractions, and why?
qa.a: Diya could cut a paper ribbon into eighths and count how many fit in three-quarters. Seeing the pieces would show why the rule works.

qa.q: How might Ma'am see Diya's mistake on the word problem?
qa.a: Ma'am probably sees that Diya knows the rule but not what it means, which is why Ma'am asked Diya to think about the meaning of the question.

grounding: A child learns flip and multiply without understanding why, gets familiar sums right, and is lost when the teacher gives a word problem in a new shape.

subtype: Approach: drawing pictures and diagrams of the idea [Action]
passage: Dear diary, Kartik here. Science homework today: parts of a plant. I read the page twice and thought, that's easy. Then I decided to draw the plant. I drew the roots first, and had to stop. What do roots look like in the soil? I added thin little hairs, because the book mentioned them, and only then thought: oh, those hairs are what drink the water. I labelled the stem, "carries water up," and the leaf, "makes food." My sister Sarika looked over, pushing back her hair. "Bhaiya, you forgot the flower!" Reading did not show me that. Drawing did. I'm going to draw the next chapter too.

qa.q: Who noticed that Kartik forgot the flower?
qa.a: His sister Sarika noticed.

qa.q: How did Kartik feel about drawing the plant, and how can you tell?
qa.a: He was pleased and curious. He decided to draw the next chapter too because drawing showed him things reading did not.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Kartik try for a diagram with many parts, and why?
qa.a: He could draw a small sketch first, then add labels one at a time. That way he does not forget a part such as the flower.

qa.q: How does Sarika see Kartik's drawing?
qa.a: Sarika looks at it with fresh eyes and quickly sees what is missing. Her remark shows the drawing is clear enough for someone else to check.

grounding: A child learning parts of a plant draws and labels what each does, and drawing makes him notice details that reading skipped.

subtype: Approach: trying easy examples first then harder ones [Action]
passage: In the school maths lab, Aryan pushed his decimals worksheet away. Sonali Ma'am slid a tray of play coins across the table. "Start small." Aryan picked up two 50-paise coins. "Half a rupee and half a rupee. That makes one rupee!" He smiled. Then he took two rupee coins and three more small ones and lined them up for 2.75, and added a rupee and fifty paise from the tray. He counted slowly. "Four rupees and twenty-five paise." He wrote 4.25 in the box. "Can I try another, Ma'am?" She nodded and pulled the tray closer.

qa.q: Which coins did Aryan pick up first?
qa.a: He picked up two 50-paise coins.

qa.q: What was Aryan feeling after he counted four rupees and twenty-five paise?
qa.a: He felt proud and encouraged. He asked for another sum straight away.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Aryan use to try harder decimals, and why?
qa.a: He could draw a number line marked in tenths and hop along it. It gives him a picture to check the answer against.

qa.q: How does Sonali Ma'am see Aryan's progress with the coins?
qa.a: Sonali Ma'am sees a boy who moved from a shove-away worksheet to asking for another sum, so the small examples worked for him.

grounding: A boy struggling with decimals starts with easy coin sums and moves to bigger ones, and each success gives him confidence to try the next.

subtype: Approach: deciding he is just bad at the subject and giving up [Pitfall]
passage: Note to Vidya's parents, Tuesday. Vidya got three fraction questions wrong one after another. She put her pencil down. "I'm not a maths person," she said. She would not try a fourth. She sat with her arms folded and looked out of the window. I sat beside her and asked her to show me the first line of the last question. She shrugged. I said the next practice would be small, one question with me, and tomorrow two. She did not answer. I think her belief may be harder to shift than the sums, so I will keep the practice short and often. Farida, teacher

qa.q: How many fraction questions did Vidya get wrong in a row?
qa.a: She got three wrong one after another.

qa.q: What does Vidya's remark "I'm not a maths person" suggest about how she felt?
qa.a: It suggests she felt discouraged and hopeless after the mistakes. Her folded arms and refusal to try a fourth question show she gave up.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Vidya try instead of giving up, and why?
qa.a: She could pick one wrong question and find the exact step where it went off. Practising that step is how the skill grows.

qa.q: How does the teacher Farida see Vidya's reaction?
qa.a: Farida sees a belief that could keep Vidya from practising, and not only a set of wrong sums. That is why Farida plans short practice with Vidya.

grounding: After three wrong answers a girl says she is not a maths person and stops trying, and this belief keeps her from the practice that would help.

subtype: Approach: asking the teacher a specific question [Revision]
passage: I'm Francis, and last week I kept getting subtraction sums wrong. I guessed a lot, and guessing did not help. One evening I took a sheet and wrote exactly where I got lost: "When the top digit is smaller, I don't know the borrowing." Papa read it and said, "That's my boy. Now you know the exact spot." Next day I showed Ira Ma'am the line. "Can you show me just this step again?" She did not do the whole page. She showed me one sum, breaking a ten into ones, and then she let me try the next. I got it right. I wrote her a thank-you note.

qa.q: What step of subtraction did Francis find hard?
qa.a: He got lost at the borrowing step, when the top digit is smaller.

qa.q: What was Francis feeling after Ira Ma'am let him try the next sum himself?
qa.a: He felt pleased and relieved when he got it right. He was so glad that he wrote her a thank-you note.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Francis use to practise borrowing after class, and why?
qa.a: He could do five borrowing sums at home and mark each himself. Repeating that one step will make it feel normal.

qa.q: How might Ira Ma'am see Francis's question?
qa.a: Ira Ma'am probably finds it easy to help, because Francis asked about one exact step instead of saying he did not understand anything.

grounding: A child notices guessing does not help, writes down that he gets lost at the borrowing step, and next day asks the teacher to show that one step.

subtype: Approach: watching a video explanation and copying the method [Action]
passage: Come, sit. I'll tell you about my niece Damini. I'm Saurabh Mama, and I watched this myself. She was ten, and the school gave her a tablet with a lesson on angles. She did not just watch it like a cartoon. After every step, she pressed pause. She took her notebook, drew the angle and copied the step. Then she looked at the video's answer and compared it with her own. Once her number was different. She said, "Hm," rewound, and saw she had read the protractor from the wrong end. She fixed it and pressed play. That is how she learned angles, one small piece at a time.

qa.q: What did Damini do after every step of the video?
qa.a: She pressed pause, drew the angle, and copied the step in her notebook.

qa.q: What might Damini have been feeling when her number was different from the video's?
qa.a: She was probably curious and a bit puzzled. Her "Hm" and the rewind show she wanted to find the difference, not to give up.

qa.q: What choice did Damini make that helped her learn, and why did it matter?
qa.a: She paused and did each step herself before going on. That way she found her own mistake with the protractor before it grew into a bigger one.

qa.q: How does Saurabh see Damini's way of watching the video?
qa.a: Saurabh saw a niece who used the tablet as a teacher, not a toy, and he remembers it as an example worth telling.

grounding: A girl watches a short video lesson on angles, pauses after each step to repeat it in her notebook, and compares her answer with the video before going on.

subtype: Approach: leaving it and returning after a rest [Revision]
passage:
"It's impossible!" Tarun glared at the triangle in his notebook. "Twenty minutes and it still doesn't work!"
"Then close the book," said his mother Neelam. "Go and play."
"But it's homework."
"It will be here when you come back."
Tarun kicked the ball around the courtyard for half an hour. When he came in, red-faced and thirsty, he picked up his pencil and looked at the figure again.
"Oh!" he said. "I wrote AB where it should be BC. I mislabelled the sides!"
He fixed them and finished the problem in five minutes.
"Ma, it was that easy."

qa.q: How long did Tarun stare at the triangle before he stopped?
qa.a: He had worked on it for twenty minutes.

qa.q: What was Tarun feeling when he said "It's impossible!"?
qa.a: He was frustrated and stuck. He glared at the notebook and thought twenty minutes should have been enough.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Tarun use the next time he is stuck, and why?
qa.a: He could check the labels on his figure and read the question again before quitting. Small slips in labelling can hide behind a problem that seems impossible.

qa.q: How does Neelam see Tarun's stuck problem?
qa.a: Neelam sees a boy who is tired and wound up, so she sends him to play, trusting the problem will look different afterwards. 😊

grounding: A boy stares at a geometry problem for twenty minutes, goes to play, and on returning sees he mislabelled the sides and finishes it in five.
